narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 66.8% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction to assess risk, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your third-year class ranking had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Placing in the first decile (bottom 10%) of your class in Year 3 is substantially lower than the average of about 5.8 among students who were accepted. Your first-year ranking was the second most important factor and also pulled the prediction toward failure; your fourth-decile placement sits well below the average of 6.0 for accepted students. These two academic performance signals outweighed everything else.

Your LSAT score of 36 was the third most important feature, but it worked in the opposite direction, modestly pulling the prediction toward passing. While helpful, it was not enough to offset the weaker class rankings.

Gender, race, family income (upper-middle bracket), undergraduate GPA, and full-time status played no meaningful role in this outcome.

You should focus on strengthening your academic record and bar-exam readiness. Consider retaking key courses, seeking structured bar-prep support, or improving your LSAT before reapplying. Many students improve their trajectory with targeted effort in these areas. (218 words)
